analysis.one_liner: Toughened Clean Water Act enforcement against polluting facilities and expanded public disclosure of polluted waters.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 25 cosponsors including 3 Republicans, died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cracked down on industrial and municipal facilities that violate their water discharge permits. It raised penalties so they exceed the money a polluter saves by breaking the rules, forced inspections of repeat violators, blocked new permits for facilities that keep violating, let citizens sue over past violations, and required signs at beaches and fishing areas where water is unsafe or fish are contaminated. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who swim, fish, or live near polluted water; communities downstream of industrial dischargers; and environmental groups that enforce the law through citizen suits.

how_it_helps.text: Requires signs at every major public access point to water that violates a quality standard or carries a fish-consumption advisory, explaining the health effects and where to get more information [S2] [S3].
Caps penalty negotiations so polluters cannot settle for less than the economic benefit they gained from violating, and sets minimum penalties for serious and repeat violations [S2] [S3].

Requires annual inspections of major dischargers, random sampling of effluent, and monthly reporting by large industrial facilities; facilities designated as 'significant noncompliers' cannot receive new permits until violations are fixed [S2] [S3].
Expands citizen lawsuits to cover past violations and makes clear that a citizen suing a polluter keeps litigation rights even if a state brings its own weaker action [S2] [S3].
Requires wastewater utilities to tell customers in their bills about where they discharge and any permit violations from the past year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Industrial facilities with water discharge permits — chemical plants, manufacturers, and other point-source dischargers — who would face higher mandatory penalties, mandatory inspections, and monthly reporting. Municipal wastewater plants face new disclosure and reporting duties.

drawbacks.text: The bill is one-sided enforcement legislation with little cost-benefit analysis; critics of strict Clean Water enforcement in the 1990s argued that mandatory minimum penalties and automatic permit denials could punish minor or technical violations and impose compliance costs that fall partly on municipal ratepayers [S3].

New duties for publicly owned treatment works — bill-stuffer disclosures, permits for industrial users, inspection authority — would add administrative costs for local utilities, though municipalities' stormwater-only discharges are exempted from the public-information requirements [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to public health and the millions of Americans who use contaminated waterways, and the bill's own findings note that citizen enforcement had already recovered $11 million in penalties and interest between fiscal 1988 and 1993 [S3]. The costs fall on violators, which the bill treats as the point: its findings state that penalties at the time were often smaller than the money polluters saved by breaking the rules [S3]. The main honest objection is that rigid minimum penalties can hit small or technical violations hard, and municipal utilities bear some compliance burdens; the bill mitigates this by exempting municipal stormwater and phasing in requirements over two to three years.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Water Resources and Environment subcommittee, and never came back out — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone of New Jersey introduced the bill on March 16, 1995, joined by ten original co-introducers including Republican Christopher Shays of Connecticut [S1] [S3].
It gathered 25 cosponsors — 21 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 1 Independent — within the 104th Congress [S4].
The House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on March 16, 1995, and to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment on March 30, 1995 [S1] [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a markup or floor vote and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that discharge pollutants into waterways are better off — they avoided mandatory minimum penalties, required inspections, permit denial for repeat violators, and expanded citizen suits. The same lenient enforcement and limited public disclosure the bill's findings criticized continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industrial polluters and weak state enforcement

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 25 cosponsors split 21 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but with Republicans holding the House majority in 1995, the bill's mostly Democratic support never translated into committee action [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Industrial dischargers (manufacturing, chemical, and other permitted facilities)
industries.note: These facilities would face mandatory minimum penalties, penalties at least equal to their economic gain from violating, annual inspections with independent sampling, monthly reporting, and permit denial for repeat violators. The bill's findings state penalties were often smaller than the economic benefit of violating, so violators profited relative to law-abiding competitors [S3].

industries.industry: Publicly owned treatment works (municipal wastewater utilities)
industries.note: Utilities would have to disclose discharge locations and violations in customer bills and obtain permits for significant industrial users, but municipal stormwater discharges are exempted from public-information rules and requirements phase in over two to three years [S3].

Expanded citizen suit rights, shorter notice periods, and EPA encouragement of citizen enforcement would give these groups more power to sue polluters, building on $11 million in penalties and interest they helped recover from 1988 to 1993 [S3].
Mandatory random effluent sampling must be analyzed by federal, state, or state-approved labs independent of the permittee, creating inspection-driven demand for independent testing [S3].
